The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and mirrors the quiet, unhurried rhythm of the river and the ferrywoman's routine. 

The "story time" covers only about half an hour—from shortly before 6:50 AM until the ferry reaches the other side of the river around 7:20 AM. Most of the narrative unfolds in "real-time" scenes through brief, grounded dialogues as each of the three passengers boards. Between these interactions, time is gently compressed (skipping the quiet minutes between 6:50, 7:05, and 7:10) and decades of history—such as the thirty-year-old schedule written by Ilse's husband and the seasonal habits of summer tourists—are effortlessly condensed into single sentences of internal reflection. 

Conversely, once the ferry leaves the dock, time is subtly stretched. The narrative slows down to focus on sensory details (the pull of the current, the sound of the cable, the call of a heron) and draws out the brief, tense moment of the vibrating phone in Ilse's pocket. This deliberate slowing of the pace enhances the atmospheric stillness of the fog and underscores Ilse's stoic, unwavering presence.
